quote: imagine that we’re going to go and survey all your students five years later, and see how many of them have lost their religions compared to a control group
content: Versions of this experiment have been run. The best-known — Gervais & Norenzayan (2012), in which analytic-thinking primes reduced religious belief — failed a direct preregistered replication (Sanchez et al., 2017) and the large Science/Nature replication project. The natural experiment of higher education is mixed: in American panel data, more education reduces belief in biblical literalism but increases religious attendance and participation (Schwadel, 2011). There is a real correlation between reflective thinking and non-belief (Pennycook et al., 2016), but the causal manipulation the essay imagines has not produced the effect it predicts.

quote: religion is a sign, a symptom, of larger problems that don’t go away just because someone loses their religion.
content: The canary metaphor takes a side in a debate the essay does not mention. The cognitive science of religion treats religious belief as a by-product of ordinary, well-functioning cognition — agency detection, teleological intuition, theory of mind — rather than of a reasoning deficit (Barrett, 2000). And the strongest predictors of how religious a population is are not measures of its reasoning but of its insecurity: across countries, religiosity falls as welfare spending rises (Gill & Lundsgaarde, 2004), the pattern Norris and Inglehart document at global scale. If that is right, the canary is measuring exposure to risk, not the sanity waterline.

quote: Could you—realistically speaking, regardless of fairness—win a Nobel while advocating the existence of Santa Claus?
content: The argument assumes its conclusion. It works only if theistic belief is epistemically equivalent to belief in Santa Claus — which is the proposition in dispute, not a premise both sides grant. Religious Nobel laureates in the sciences are not rare exceptions to be explained away: William Phillips (Physics 1997), Charles Townes (Physics 1964) and Arthur Schawlow (Physics 1981) all spoke publicly of their faith, and surveys of scientists at elite American universities find roughly a third holding some belief in God (Ecklund & Scheitle, 2007). The inference from “some excellent scientists are religious” to “the sanity waterline is ridiculously low even in the highest halls” needs the equivalence it smuggles in.
